title: What the homepage has to prove for an accounting firm
metaTitle: Accounting firm homepage: who, and for whom
excerpt: An accounting firm homepage should name who does the work, for which kind of company, and how to book a call. A skyline and the word excellence do not.
alt: A close view of a smartphone home screen filled with app icons on a pale table, a first glance as crowded as a homepage that never names a person.
caption: A phone full of icons, waiting for one of them to say what it is. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should an accounting firm put on its homepage first?
faqs.answer: Name who does the work and what kind of company they do it for, then offer a way to book a call. A founder looking for a calm expert uses those facts to decide whether to stay. A skyline and a claim of excellence do not answer either question.

faqs.question: Can one homepage speak to every type of client?
faqs.answer: Lead with one or two kinds of company you actually want, such as owner-led product companies or independent clinics. Link other work in plain language. Averaging everyone into businesses of all sizes makes the right founder feel unseen.

faqs.question: What should the booking button say?
faqs.answer: Say book a call, and add what the call is for and how long it is if that is stable. A fit check on the books, the entity, and the timing is a clear promise. Learn more, and submit, leave the founder to guess what happens next.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
An accounting firm homepage has one job for a founder who needs a calm expert. It shows who does the work and for whom, and it offers a way to book a call. Write the page in that order. A skyline and the word excellence do not name a person, and they do not name a kind of company.

This buyer is often a founder with a messy year, a raise coming, or a tax notice they do not want to interpret alone. They are looking for someone steady, not a performance of scale. Nielsen Norman Group's review of page visits puts the first 10 seconds at the center of the decision to stay, and notes that people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds. Google's helpful-content guidance gives extra weight to trust on topics that affect financial stability. An accounting homepage is that kind of page. The first screen has to be specific enough to trust.

## Who, and for whom, before anything else

Who means a person. A name, a role, and the work they actually do. "Mina Alvarez, who closes the books and prepares the return for owner-led companies." If several people share the work, name the one a founder will meet on the first call, and say what the others do. "Our team of professionals" is a hallway with the lights off.

For whom means the kind of company, in words a founder uses. Product companies past the first hire. Clinics with a handful of practitioners. Shops with inventory. Studios and agencies that invoice in projects. Trades with job costs. Pick the ones you truly want. A founder should be able to see themselves, or see that they are in the wrong place, without a quiz.

Put those two facts in the first view, then the call. "Book a call" should say what the call is. Thirty minutes to see if the books, the entity, and the timing fit. Not a demo of software. Not a lecture. A fit check with the person who would do the work.

If you only have room for one sentence, make it the who and the for whom together. "Mina closes the books for owner-led product companies." The skyline can wait forever.

## What a founder is trying to feel, and what they need to know

Calm is a property of the facts, not of a soft photograph. A founder relaxes when they learn that a named person has done this shape of work for a company of their shape, and that they can talk to that person without a scavenger hunt.

They need a few practical facts near the top, after the sentence. Which entities you are glad to take. Companies, sole traders, partnerships, trusts, if those are real for your practice and your license. Which accounting tools you already work in, such as the ledger they are likely to have open. Whether you do the monthly books, the annual return, a cleanup, or the conversations with a future investor. You do not need all of those in the hero. You need the one that matches the practice.

They do not need a sermon on the importance of compliance. They already know a bad year is expensive. Repeating the fear is not calm. State the work and the boundary. "We do not take listed companies." "We do not replace your lawyer." "We will not file a return we have not had time to understand." Those sentences lower the temperature because they show judgment.

Leave the word excellence off the page. It is the verbal version of a glass tower. Every firm in the search results can claim it, so it sorts nobody. If you need a standard, write the standard. "You get management numbers you can read, and a person who will explain the line you ask about." That is a promise a founder can test on the call.

## The order of the first screen

Build the phone screen before the wide one. A founder will often open this between product work and a payroll worry.

1. Who does the work, and for whom.
2. A button to book a call, with one line about length and purpose.
3. One photograph of that person, or of the room the call represents, cropped so the face or the desk is visible. Not a skyline.
4. One boundary. The company size, the entity, or the work you do not take.

Under that, two or three offers in the founder's language. Monthly books. A cleanup before a raise. The annual return. A quarterly look at cash. Each with who does it. The pricing page can hold the shape of the fee. The homepage should not become a rate card, and it should not hide the fact that a fee exists.

Then a short note on what to have ready for the call. Entity type. Roughly how the books are kept. The question they want answered. Last year's return if they have it. The point is to make the call useful, not to run an audit through a form.

End by repeating the booking. People who scroll are the ones Nielsen describes as having stayed past the harsh first seconds. Give them the same action, not a new slogan.

## Why a skyline and "excellence" fail this buyer

A skyline says the firm is in a city, or wishes to look as if it were in a larger one. A founder who needs a calm expert is not hiring the skyline. They are hiring a person who will not dramatize a messy ledger. The photograph of the tower pushes the name and the client type down the page, which is exactly the information that had to land inside 10 seconds.

Excellence fails as a claim because it cannot be checked. Trust, in Google's framing, is the part of experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trust that matters most, and the others feed it. A name and a client type are checkable on a call. An adjective is not. On a topic that touches financial stability, an unchecked adjective is a weak opening.

The same failure shows up as glass, marble lobbies, and drones over the river. They are the costume of a firm that wants to look large. Some founders want large. The founder in this article wants calm and fit. If your practice really is a large firm with a named partner for this segment, say the partner's name and the segment. The building can be the last photograph, or none.

Watch the headline for a cousin of the same mistake. "Your growth partner." "Numbers that empower." "Financial clarity for the journey." None of those name who, or for whom. Replace them with the person and the company type. You can sound like an adult without sounding like a billboard.

## What the rest of the homepage may add

Once the first screen is honest, add only facts that change the booking.

How the relationship usually starts. A cleanup, then monthly books, then the return. Or a return only, for founders who already have a bookkeeper. Say which of those you want. A homepage that offers everything at equal volume is a directory, and a tired founder will not build the package for you.

The tools and the rhythm. "We work in the ledger you already use, and you see the same close each month." Name the tool if you are glad to be hired for it. Do not name eight tools to look flexible if you are excellent in one. There is that word again. Say "we know this ledger well" instead.

A single proof point you can publish. The kind of company, the constraint, the decision. Not a fake testimonial, and not a revenue number you are not allowed to share. If you have no proof you can print, do not invent a percentage. The named person is already a form of proof. A fabricated growth stat is a way to lose the calm buyer the moment they notice.

A plain sentence on licenses and who signs the work, in the language your regulator expects. Founders who have been burned look for that. Put it where they can find it without a hunt, and do not let it crowd out the name.

## How to review the opening

Give the live page, on a phone, to a founder or to someone playing one. Ten seconds. Then ask who would do the work, what kind of company it is for, and how they would book a call.

If they say "a big firm" or "finance," the skyline and the adjective won. If they name a role and a company type, and they can find the call, the page is doing its job. If they ask whether you are selling software, the button or the hero image looks like a product launch. Change it to a person.

Read the first screen with the photographs covered. The sentences should still sort the buyer. Then uncover the photographs. If they contradict the sentences, reshoot or recrop. A calm claim next to a dramatic city is an argument with itself.

Jakob Nielsen's practical line, in that Nielsen Norman Group article, is that you must communicate the value within 10 seconds to earn several minutes. Here the value is a person, a kind of company, and a call.

## When the firm serves more than one kind of founder

Say so without averaging them into "businesses of all sizes." Two clear kinds beat one foggy kind. "Owner-led product companies, and independent clinics." Give each a line and a path to the same booking, and say if different people lead them. A founder of a clinic should not have to wonder if they will be treated as a startup on the call.

If you also do personal tax for individuals, decide whether this homepage is for them. Mixing a founder's books and a family's return on one hero makes both audiences feel secondary. Give the secondary work a link with a plain label. Keep the hero for the buyer you wrote this page to win.

The next page that founder opens, once they believe a person might fit, is often the one about money. They want the shape of the fee before they put a messy year on a calendar. Read [how to show fit on the pricing page](/blog/a-pricing-page-for-an-accounting-firm) before you publish a rate card that only says to get in touch.
